description: Modelled on the 1973 UC Berkeley graduate admissions case (Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, Science, 1975). The numbers here are synthetic, for a fictional university. Pooled, men were admitted at 44.7% and women at 30.7%, yet in all six departments women were admitted at the same or a slightly higher rate. Women applied mostly to the most selective departments (English admits about 9%, Psychology about 25%), while men crowded into Engineering and Physics, which admit about 60%. Group the admit rate by department and gender, or control for department in a logistic regression, and the gap vanishes or reverses. The confounder is department: Simpson's paradox.
hints: One pooled percentage can hide what is happening inside the groups it lumps together. Don't stop at the headline number. Break the comparison down by the other categorical columns.
Compute the admit rate for each gender within each department (groupby(['department', 'gender'])['admitted'].mean()). Then look at where men and women actually applied.

In every department women are admitted at the same or a higher rate. They simply applied mostly to the selective departments (English admits about 9%, Engineering about 63%). The department mix is a confounder that creates the pooled gap. It is Simpson's paradox, and the answer is department.
